Your brain uses volume as its primary cue for deciding what is foreground, what is background. So, louder is up front, foreground, and things we hear as quieter are going to be background, support. Every engineer is fighting for that perceived loudness edge on Spotify, and most people are chasing the same tools: better limiters, more compressors, better loudness. It's called the LUFS gate, and once you understand how to use it, you can make your master sound louder. Before I show you the trick, I need to give you a super quick explanation of how Spotify or any streaming service actually measures your song's loudness. Because once you get this, the whole thing will click. You probably heard the term LUFS thrown around. LUFS stands for loudness units full scale. All it really means is how loud does your song actually sound to the human ear, on average, over the entire track. It's not measuring your loudest moments, it's measuring the whole picture of the song. And you might have heard people say, "Just master to -14 LUFS and you're good." But, that's not how the real world works. Pull up any major release right now, hip-hop, pop, EDM, those masters are sitting at -7, maybe -8, possibly even -6 LUFS. Engineers are still mastering loud. So, the goal is to get your master as loud and competitive as possible, and then make sure Spotify is measuring it as favorably as it can. And that's where the LUFS gate comes in. Here's the thing most people don't know. The way LUFS is calculated, there is a built-in gate in the measurement. If a section of your song is too quiet, soft intro, or breakdown, or the fade out, the section gets excluded from the loudness calculation entirely. It just doesn't count. So, take a hard-hitting hip-hop track that opens with 8 seconds of a quiet intro. Spotify's meter is running the whole time, but that intro is getting thrown out of the measurement. Those soft moments are secretly inflating your number, and Spotify is using the inflated number to decide how loud to play your song. Recommendations for a fully mono low end originated in vinyl mastering, where excessive bass level or side channel low-frequency information could cause problems. The mono bass argument was further promoted by the fact that PA rigs typically have their subs configured in mono. The process of monoing the low end involved using a high-pass filter on the side channel to filter out low-frequency content. This is sometimes referred to as an elliptical filter. For the purposes of this video, I'm going to refer to that process as hard monoing the low end. Hard monoing the low end has several potential downsides, though. First is an increase in peak level. Second is phase smearing. If you're using a nonlinear phase filter on the side channel, then you can smear the phase relationship between mid and side, right in the critical bass region where phase coherence is so important. The third is that you can experience level loss. If you remove information in the side channel, then overall bass level can drop. Fourth is you can have timbral changes. If there's information that exists only in the side channel—which is otherwise known as antiphase content—by removing that, you're actually removing detail and not just level. I think the key for me with mixed compression is getting your attack and release settings right. Because I think a lot of people assume that because it's mixed compression and you just want to be stopping overloads that you have to have a fast attack and release. Whereas I don't see it like that at all. I just want it there to help glue and to help just the feel of the sound of a compressor on the mix. It's more about lifting some of the detail out than it is about stopping those transients. So I always have quite a slow attack, which allows me to have to keep the transients happening. Especially in the low end, you've got to make sure you don't have too hard an attack. Otherwise, you just lose all that thump in the mix. So even though you're... you can be compressing quite a bit, but with a slower attack, it's a lot more gentle and you're still getting the transients through.
